code.title: Toy pipeline: bytecode, feedback, hot tier, deopt

followUps:
OSR (on-stack replacement) swaps a running function from slow code to faster code in the middle of its execution. It is needed because a loop can get hot while the function is still on its first call, so waiting for the next call would never help.

Example: function f(){ for(let i=0;i<1e8;i++) s+=i } is called once. V8 notices the loop back-edge counter, compiles an optimized version, and jumps into it at the current iteration, carrying the live variables across.

The interpreter is kept because it starts instantly and uses little memory, and most code runs only once or twice. Compiling everything to machine code up front would cost more time and memory than it saves.

It also collects the type feedback that the optimizer needs, and it is the safe place to land when optimized code deoptimizes. A function called once during startup should never pay for TurboFan, which can take milliseconds per function.

Code caching lets the browser reuse compiled bytecode instead of parsing and compiling the same script again. On a repeat visit the scanner, parser and bytecode generator steps are largely skipped, so startup is faster.

Chrome typically caches after the script has run a few times and stores the result with the resource. Only bytecode is cached, not optimized machine code or feedback, so the hot code still warms up from Ignition each time. A changed file produces a new cache entry.

Compiling everything eagerly wastes time and memory on code that never runs, and it delays the first useful work. Eager optimized code is also built without type feedback, so it would guess types badly.

Example: a page ships 2 MB of JavaScript but uses 15% on load. Lazy parsing and an interpreter start-up path pay only for that 15%. The trade is that the first calls are slower, which hot-code tiering recovers.

Warm-up is the period where code runs in the interpreter and is still being compiled by higher tiers, so it is slower than steady state. A benchmark that includes it measures compilation, not your algorithm.

Example: the first 1,000 calls may take 5 ms each, later calls 0.2 ms. Run a few hundred untimed iterations first, then time batches. Report cold start separately when start-up speed is what matters, as it is for CLIs and serverless functions.

code.title: Hidden classes: which objects share a Map

followUps:
Deleting the last-added property is cheap, because V8 can step back to the previous hidden class in the transition tree. Deleting a middle property usually forces the object into slow dictionary mode.

Example: o={a:1,b:2,c:3}; delete o.c returns to the shape with a and b. But delete o.a breaks the slot layout, so the object becomes a hash table and every access is slower. Prefer o.a = undefined or null, or rebuild the object without the key.

Class fields declared in the class body are initialised in a fixed order for every instance, so all instances follow the same transitions and share one hidden class.

Example: class P { x = 0; y = 0; } gives every instance the shape {x, y}, even if the constructor later assigns different values. Fields you only add conditionally in methods create extra shapes, so declare every field up front, using null as the empty value.

In Node you can ask V8 directly, using a debug-only native function. Run with --allow-natives-syntax and call %HaveSameMap(a, b), which returns true when both objects share a map.

// node --allow-natives-syntax t.js
const a = {x:1, y:2}, b = {x:3, y:4};
console.log(%HaveSameMap(a, b)); // true

In DevTools, a heap snapshot lists objects grouped by constructor, and %DebugPrint(obj) prints the map address. Do not ship natives in production code.

code.title: Inline cache states: mono, poly, megamorphic

followUps:
No, megamorphic is not always bad. It is a cost you notice only on hot paths, and for code that runs rarely, or that genuinely handles many types (a generic toString or a serializer), it is fine.

The loss is that V8 uses a slower shared stub cache, and optimizing compilers cannot inline a fixed-offset load. A loop doing 100 million accesses can be several times slower; a handler that runs 100 times will not matter. Measure before restructuring.

Inlining needs a monomorphic or small polymorphic call site, because the compiler must know which function and which shapes to specialise for. If the site is megamorphic, V8 usually cannot inline the callee, so the call stays a real call.

Example: area(s) that sees only Circles can be inlined and its shape check hoisted. Once it sees six shapes, the call remains and every property read goes through the generic path. Inlining and IC state are the same speculation seen from two sides.

Methods live on the prototype, so a call like obj.speak() is cached by the IC using the receiver's hidden class plus a check that the prototype chain has not changed.

Steps: the IC checks obj's map, then V8 knows (from a validity cell) that the prototype still holds the same method, so it loads the function directly. If you patch Class.prototype.speak later, the cell is invalidated and cached code is dropped. Avoid mutating prototypes in hot code.

code.title: Speculation guard and deoptimization

followUps:
When inlined functions deopt, V8 rebuilds one interpreter frame per inlined function, so the stack looks as if nothing had been inlined. The optimizer records a frame state (which values live in which registers or stack slots) at each point that can deopt.

The deoptimizer reads these values, creates the Ignition frames, and resumes at the matching bytecode offset. Example: if f inlines g and g's guard fails, you get a frame for g on top of a frame for f, and execution continues in g.

try/catch stopped being a deopt reason because TurboFan, introduced in Chrome 59, can optimize functions that contain it. The old Crankshaft compiler simply refused such functions.

The practical advice is now different: you do not need to move try/catch into a separate helper for speed. Throwing exceptions is still slow compared with return values, so do not use them for ordinary control flow in a hot loop.

"Insufficient type feedback" means the code ran too little, or never reached that spot, so the feedback vector has no data about the types there. The optimizer cannot guess, so it emits a deopt point.

Example: if (rare) { x.y } inside an optimized function. The branch was never executed, so when it first runs V8 deoptimizes (a soft deopt), collects feedback, and re-optimizes later with the real types. One such deopt is normal.

code.title: Primitives are immutable; closures keep locals alive

followUps:
Pointer compression stores heap pointers as 32-bit offsets from a base address instead of 64-bit pointers, which cuts V8 heap memory by roughly 30 to 40 percent.

Consequences: tagged words are 4 bytes, Smis became 31-bit integers, and the heap is capped at about 4 GB per isolate cage. Chrome has used it since version 80. Node does not enable it by default, because many servers need heaps larger than the cap.

A number is boxed when it cannot be a Smi, meaning it is a fraction or larger than the Smi range, and the engine has no unboxed slot for it. It is then allocated as a HeapNumber object.

Examples: 1.5 and 2**40 are boxed when stored in a generic object field, while 42 is not. Optimized code may keep a double in a register unboxed, and double arrays and typed arrays store raw doubles. Boxing in a hot loop creates garbage, which is why numeric kernels use typed arrays.

A substring can keep a large string alive because V8 may represent it as a sliced string, a small object that points into the parent instead of copying characters. While the slice is reachable, the whole parent stays in memory.

Example: reading a 50 MB log and keeping line.slice(0, 10) for 1,000 lines can retain all 50 MB. Typical fix is to force a copy, for example by flattening with (' ' + s).slice(1) or re-joining, only when you must keep short pieces of a huge text for a long time.

code.title: Tracing GC: mark from roots, sweep the rest
code.python:
# Tracing GC idea: mark everything reachable from the roots, free the rest (cycles included).
refs = [[1], [2], [1], [4], [3], []]        # object i points to the objects listed
roots = [0]
marked = [False] * len(refs)
stack = list(roots)                          # mark phase: depth-first from the roots
while stack:
    o = stack.pop()
    if marked[o]:
        continue
    marked[o] = True
    stack.extend(refs[o])
live = [i for i, m in enumerate(marked) if m]       # sweep phase: unmarked objects are garbage
freed = [i for i, m in enumerate(marked) if not m]
print("references: [[1],[2],[1],[4],[3],[]] roots: [0]")
print("live:", ",".join(map(str, live)))
print("freed:", ",".join(map(str, freed)), "(3 and 4 point at each other but no root reaches them)")

followUps:
A scavenge is cheap because it copies only the live objects and never even looks at the dead ones. If 95 percent of new objects die young, the work is proportional to the surviving 5 percent.

Example: a 16 MB semi-space with 800 KB of survivors copies 800 KB, then the whole space is reused by resetting one allocation pointer. Compare mark-sweep, which has to examine every object. This is why short-lived temporary objects are nearly free in V8.

Premature promotion is when an object that would soon die gets moved into old space too early, so it is later cleaned by the slower major GC instead of a cheap scavenge.

It happens when the young generation is too small or an allocation burst fills it, for example 20 MB of per-request objects with a 16 MB semi-space. The objects survive two scavenges only because the request is still running. Symptoms are frequent mark-compact runs and growing old space. Raising the semi-space size often helps.

--max-semi-space-size sets the size of the young generation's semi-spaces, and --max-old-space-size sets the maximum old-generation heap in megabytes. Both change the GC frequency and memory ceiling.

Larger semi-space: fewer scavenges and less premature promotion, but more memory. Old space limit: when reached, Node dies with "heap out of memory", and when set too high for a container, the OS kills it first. Example: node --max-old-space-size=1536 app.js in a 2 GB container.

code.title: Listener leak and AbortController fix

followUps:
AbortController lets you remove many listeners and cancel async work with one call, because they all share one signal. You no longer need to keep a reference to each handler to call removeEventListener.

const ctl = new AbortController();
window.addEventListener('resize', onResize, { signal: ctl.signal });
socket.addEventListener('message', onMsg, { signal: ctl.signal });
// on unmount:
ctl.abort(); // removes both

The same signal also cancels fetch.

WeakMap is the right tool when you attach extra data to an object you do not own and the data should disappear when that object does. Keys are held weakly, so the entry never keeps the key alive.

Example: a cache of computed layout per DOM node, cache.set(node, layout). When the node is removed and unreachable, the entry is collected, with no cleanup code. Do not use it when you need to list entries, count them, or use string keys.

The simplest regression test repeats the suspect action many times, forces garbage collection, and checks that memory or object counts do not grow. Run it in Node with --expose-gc.

for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) openAndClose();
global.gc();
const base = process.memoryUsage().heapUsed;
for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) openAndClose();
global.gc();
assert(process.memoryUsage().heapUsed - base < 2e6);

For browsers, memlab automates the same idea.

code.title: Three-snapshot growth check for a leak

followUps:
Shallow size is the memory of the object itself; retained size is everything that would be freed if that object were removed, including objects only it keeps alive. Retained size is the one to sort by when hunting leaks.

Example: an array holding 1,000 objects of 100 bytes each has a shallow size of about 8 KB (the slots) but a retained size of roughly 108 KB. A tiny listener closure that holds a 5 MB buffer has a small shallow size and a 5 MB retained size.

You repeat the action several times (like 7) because a single run includes one-time costs: lazy initialisation, caches filling, JIT code and first-use allocations. Those look like growth but are not leaks.

A real leak adds the same amount each round. Example: if every round adds 7 objects, 7 rounds shows 49 leaked objects, a clear signal, while a one-off 1 MB lazy cache is noise. Take snapshots after the first warm-up round and compare later rounds.

A leak in a Web Worker is investigated in that worker's own heap, not the page's. The main page's snapshot will not show its objects, and workers do not share the JS heap with the page.

In Chrome DevTools, select the worker in the Memory panel's target dropdown (or open it through chrome://inspect) and take snapshots there. Also look at messages: values sent by postMessage are copied, and un-transferred large buffers or never-removed onmessage handlers are common culprits.

code.title: Flat heapUsed while Buffers grow

followUps:
A heap snapshot freezes the JS thread, can take seconds to minutes, and needs memory about equal to the heap size, so it is risky on a service that is already near its limit.

Example: a 1.5 GB heap may stall for 10 to 30 seconds and need another 1.5 GB, which can trigger the OOM kill you wanted to avoid. Mitigate: take it on one instance removed from the load balancer, and treat the file as sensitive, since it contains raw strings such as tokens and user data.

Each worker thread has its own V8 isolate, so its own heap, and the memory adds up per worker rather than being shared. Ten workers with 100 MB heaps use about 1 GB, plus per-thread overhead.

Resource limits can be set per worker, for example new Worker(f, { resourceLimits: { maxOldGenerationSizeMb: 128 } }). Messages are copied unless transferred or shared through SharedArrayBuffer. Size the pool to your memory budget, not just to the CPU count.

MaxListenersExceededWarning tells you that more than 10 listeners (the default) were added to one EventEmitter for the same event. It is an early hint of a probable listener leak, often a handler added on every request but never removed.

Example: calling socket.on('data', h) inside a request handler adds one more listener per request, so after 11 requests the warning appears. Find the emitter in the warning's stack trace and add a matching off or use once. Do not just raise the limit.

code.title: WeakMap metadata and WeakRef cache

followUps:
A WeakMap value that points back at its own key is not a leak, because the value is only reachable through the key. If nothing else reaches the key, both become garbage together.

This works because WeakMap entries are ephemerons: the value counts as alive only while the key is alive. Example: const o = {}; wm.set(o, {owner: o}). When o goes out of scope, the pair is freed. A plain Map would keep both forever.

Objects, and since ES2023 non-registered symbols, can be WeakMap keys, but primitives such as strings and numbers cannot. Using one throws a TypeError.

The reason is that primitives have no identity: 'a' is equal to every other 'a', so there is no object whose death could be observed. Example: new WeakMap().set('id', 1) throws "Invalid value used as weak map key". If you need string keys, use a Map and bound it, or wrap the key in an object.

Build it as a Map from key to WeakRef, and recreate the value when deref() returns undefined. Optionally add a FinalizationRegistry to delete dead keys so the Map does not grow.

const map = new Map();
const reg = new FinalizationRegistry(k => map.delete(k));
function put(k, v) { map.set(k, new WeakRef(v)); reg.register(v, k); }
function get(k) { return map.get(k)?.deref(); }

Treat a miss as normal: the value is recomputed.

code.title: Holey vs packed arrays

followUps:
The elements-kind lattice is the ordered set of array storage types V8 uses, and an array can only move down it, never back up. The order is PACKED_SMI, then PACKED_DOUBLE, then PACKED_ELEMENTS, and each has a HOLEY version.

Example: [1,2,3] is PACKED_SMI; pushing 1.5 makes it PACKED_DOUBLE; pushing a string makes it PACKED_ELEMENTS. Creating a hole, for example a[10] = 1 on a length-3 array, makes it HOLEY. Packed kinds allow the fastest code.

No, Array.from({length: n}) creates real elements, each set to undefined, not holes. The result is a normal array that can be iterated by forEach, map and for...of.

Example: Array.from({length:3}) gives [undefined, undefined, undefined] and 0 in arr is true, whereas new Array(3) has none (0 in arr is false). The mapping form, Array.from({length:n}, (_, i) => i), is the usual way to get a pre-sized, filled array.

Typed arrays keep raw numbers in one off-heap-style buffer, so the GC sees one object, not millions of elements, and it never scans or moves the numbers. That means far less GC work.

Example: a Float64Array(1e6) is 8 MB in one block, while an array of a million boxed doubles may need many HeapNumber objects. Writing a float to a typed array allocates nothing. The cost is fixed length and fixed element type.

code.title: Fair micro-benchmark harness

followUps:
GC can skew results because allocation-heavy code creates garbage that gets collected later, possibly during another variant's turn. The cost can land on the wrong variant.

Example: variant A allocates 200 MB of temporary arrays and variant B allocates nothing. A GC triggered while B runs makes B look slower. Fix: run each variant in its own batch with a similar warm state, watch --trace-gc, and where possible run each variant in a separate process.

The first variant often looks slower because it pays for cold caches, lazy compilation and heap growth that later variants no longer pay. The engine is still warming up when it runs.

Example: the first measured function takes 12 ms and an identical copy run second takes 8 ms. Randomise or rotate the order, do untimed warm-up of all variants, and compare medians of several rounds instead of one run.

A micro-benchmark is the wrong tool when the code is not on the hot path, or when the real cost depends on whole-program effects such as I/O, GC pressure, cache misses or real input sizes.

Example: replacing forEach with a for loop to save 20 ns per call does nothing for an API whose time is 200 ms of database waiting. Use a profiler (--cpu-prof or the Performance panel) on the real workload first, and micro-benchmark only the proven hotspot.
